passages.heading: based-on-madhyasth-darshan-so-that-organisations-sustain-and-members-are-not-instrumentalised
passages.section: Based on Madhyasth Darshan — so that organisations sustain and members are not instrumentalised
passages.text: Based on Madhyasth Darshan — so that organisations sustain and members are not instrumentalised

passages.heading: based-on-madhyasth-darshan-so-that-organisations-sustain-and-members-are-not-instrumentalised
passages.section: Based on Madhyasth Darshan — so that organisations sustain and members are not instrumentalised
passages.text: The question: must organisations be built on fear or accumulation, or is there a basis on which they sustain and their members are not used as instruments?

passages.heading: based-on-madhyasth-darshan-so-that-organisations-sustain-and-members-are-not-instrumentalised
passages.section: Based on Madhyasth Darshan — so that organisations sustain and members are not instrumentalised
passages.text: This study takes the near-universal history of human organisation — grouping for safety, sustenance, protection, shared belief, and finally wealth and power — and asks whether every such basis reduces to fear and accumulation, and whether that reduction explains two recurring failures together: members treated as instruments, and organisations that dissolve once the founding fear passes or the accumulation stalls. Against that pattern it sets Madhyasth Darshan’s alternative — organisation around understood coexistence: shared cause, goal, and programme; values fulfilled in relationships; prosperity through right-use rather than accumulation; and understanding transmitted to every member through education-sanskar. The design is argued to be coherent but is untested at civilisational scale, and its deepest premises are asserted rather than demonstrated (§10).

passages.heading: based-on-madhyasth-darshan-so-that-organisations-sustain-and-members-are-not-instrumentalised
passages.section: Based on Madhyasth Darshan — so that organisations sustain and members are not instrumentalised
passages.text: This is an applied study: it instantiates the general assembly template of coexistence in the concrete case of human organisations. The ontological account — units, saturation, orders, relationships, values, composition, and transmission — is developed in The Ontology of Coexistence and in the primary Madhyasth Darshan texts (MVD, SB, JV). This paper does not re-derive those foundations; it applies them and cites them where they carry the argument.

passages.heading: glossary-of-key-terms
passages.text: Glossary of key terms

passages.heading: glossary-of-key-terms
passages.text: Term Meaning in this paper Jeevan The sentient self, distinct from the body; the seat of desire, thought, and understanding. Coexistence (sah-astitva) Existence as units submerged in all-pervading space — distinct, energised, related; the darshan’s account of reality itself. Resolution (samadhan) The state in which every why and how one lives by is answered; understanding without residue. Right-use (sadupyog) Use of body, mind, and wealth for their purpose, as against consumption or hoarding. Education-sanskar The paired institution of teaching (education) and formation of disposition (sanskar) by which understanding is transmitted across generations. Undivided society (akhand samaj) Humankind as one society, not finally divided into sects, classes, or nations. Universal orderliness (sarvabhaum vyavastha) Self-organising governance scaling from family to world. Dharma-niti / Rajya-niti Moral policy (right-use of body, mind, wealth) and state policy (security of the same). Awakening (jagriti) Living from correct understanding, evidenced in conduct. Instrumentalised Treated as a means — net-extracted-from — rather than as an end (this paper’s term, not the texts’).

passages.heading: 1-the-central-question
passages.text: 1. The central question

passages.heading: 1-the-central-question
passages.text: Reviewing history, humans have organised in a near-universal sequence — around safety, sustenance, protection, shared belief, and finally wealth and power. §2 traces this sequence in the sources.

passages.heading: 1-the-central-question
passages.text: The question of this paper: is this the only way to form human organisations? Any better answer must meet two design objectives together:

passages.heading: 1-the-central-question
passages.text: Objective 1 — members are not instrumentalised. People in the organisation are happy and do not feel “used” by the system.

passages.heading: 1-the-central-question
passages.text: Objective 2 — the organisation sustains. It remains orderly and alive over long periods, across generations.

passages.heading: 1-the-central-question
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan answers No, this is not the only way — and claims the two objectives are met together or not at all.

passages.heading: 1-the-central-question
passages.text: The argument of the paper in one diagram:

passages.heading: 2-the-historic-pattern-and-its-common-root
passages.section: 2. The historic pattern and its common root
passages.text: 2. The historic pattern and its common root

passages.heading: 2-the-historic-pattern-and-its-common-root
passages.section: 2. The historic pattern and its common root
passages.text: SB’s History of Humans as well as JV, tell the story of how humans organized themselves as a sequence of ages — each stage formed to answer a felt lack, each stage leaving that lack unresolved.

passages.heading: 2-the-historic-pattern-and-its-common-root
passages.section: 2. The historic pattern and its common root
passages.text: In the jungle and stone ages, fear of nature and wild animals drove the first groupings. Forest, food, and shelter became the first wealth. Humans then submitted to monarchs. SB records that “The submission age was accepted based on assurances of … comfort by the monarch” (SB, Ch. 2); JV adds that the promise was never kept:

passages.heading: 2-the-historic-pattern-and-its-common-root
passages.section: 2. The historic pattern and its common root
passages.text: “The promise was that the king would ensure the security of life and property, but that hasn’t happened until now. Life and property remain insecure; peace and harmony are further still.” - JV

passages.heading: 2-the-historic-pattern-and-its-common-root
passages.section: 2. The historic pattern and its common root
passages.text: Theocratic states and idealism came next. JV recounts that idealism imposed “dos and don’ts, labelling non-believers as sinners and subjecting them to harassment, as documented in history” (JV, Ch. 1). Materialism followed — which “in practice, became caught in the cycle of accumulation” (SB, Ch. 2) — and power-centric rule built on monopoly.

passages.heading: 2-the-historic-pattern-and-its-common-root
passages.section: 2. The historic pattern and its common root
passages.text: The darshan’s central diagnostic claim is that all five bases reduce to two intertwined roots — fear and accumulation:

passages.heading: 2-the-historic-pattern-and-its-common-root
passages.section: 2. The historic pattern and its common root
passages.text: “Only three causes are observed for all the fear in humans: (1) Fear of natural events (2) Fear of animals (3) Fear of inhumaneness in humans.” - MVD, Ch. 5

passages.heading: 2-the-historic-pattern-and-its-common-root
passages.section: 2. The historic pattern and its common root
passages.text: “The lust for accumulation does not lead to satisfaction, because there is no end to accumulation.” - MVD, Ch. 12

passages.heading: 2-the-historic-pattern-and-its-common-root
passages.section: 2. The historic pattern and its common root
passages.text: The mapping is direct. Organising for safety and under monarchs is organising around fear — of nature, of animals, of other humans and groups. Organising for food, shelter, and wealth is organising around accumulation. Organising around shared belief trades on both: fear of sin, death, or damnation on one side, and accumulation of merit or salvation on the other. The power-centric economy, finally, is accumulation guarded by force — that is, by fear.

passages.heading: 2-the-historic-pattern-and-its-common-root
passages.section: 2. The historic pattern and its common root
passages.text: Every stage is reactive. Humans organise against something feared or for something accumulated. The organising principle is never the human relationship itself; it is always an external threat or an external object.

passages.heading: 3-why-such-organisations-instrumentalise-their-members
passages.section: 3. Why such organisations instrumentalise their members
passages.text: 3. Why such organisations instrumentalise their members

passages.heading: 3-why-such-organisations-instrumentalise-their-members
passages.section: 3. Why such organisations instrumentalise their members
passages.text: If an organisation is held together by fear and accumulation, its members are inevitably treated as means — instruments for producing safety or wealth for someone else. The darshan defines this with unusual precision:

passages.heading: 3-why-such-organisations-instrumentalise-their-members
passages.section: 3. Why such organisations instrumentalise their members
passages.text: “Nurturing (poshan): Unit + Conducive unit.” - MVD, Ch. 3

passages.heading: 3-why-such-organisations-instrumentalise-their-members
passages.section: 3. Why such organisations instrumentalise their members
passages.text: “Exploitation (shoshan): Unit - Conducive unit.” - MVD, Ch. 3

passages.heading: 3-why-such-organisations-instrumentalise-their-members
passages.section: 3. Why such organisations instrumentalise their members
passages.text: Exploitation subtracts from the other; nurturing adds. And:

passages.heading: 3-why-such-organisations-instrumentalise-their-members
passages.section: 3. Why such organisations instrumentalise their members
passages.text: “To disregard sentiments (values) in a relationship is indeed exploitation of that relationship.” - MVD, Ch. 16

passages.heading: 3-why-such-organisations-instrumentalise-their-members
passages.section: 3. Why such organisations instrumentalise their members
passages.text: “No human wants their own exploitation.” - MVD, Ch. 16

passages.heading: 3-why-such-organisations-instrumentalise-their-members
passages.section: 3. Why such organisations instrumentalise their members
passages.text: In the template of coexistence these are not loose metaphors. Every unit stands in relationships — mutualities whose expectations are predetermined toward completeness — and in looser contacts, whose expectations are voluntary (MVD, Ch. 4; MVD, pp. 61–62). Formally an organisation is mostly a contact: people join and leave by choice. But it is built out of, and imposes demands on, real relationships, and the value (mulya) owed in any relationship is its essentiality — what the parties reciprocate and mutually recognise (The Ontology of Coexistence §1.6). To disregard that value is, by the definition above, exploitation. This is exactly why a purely voluntary, contractual contact can still instrumentalise its members: consenting to join does not license disregard of the relationship-values the contact carries.

passages.heading: 3-why-such-organisations-instrumentalise-their-members
passages.section: 3. Why such organisations instrumentalise their members
passages.text: Profit-bound organisations must extract more from members than they return, because profit is defined as that very imbalance — “Getting higher value in exchange for lower value itself is profit” (MVD, Ch. 4) — and “No one is happy from earning obtained through exploitation” (MVD, Ch. 13). The political form of instrumentalisation is rule itself:

passages.heading: 3-why-such-organisations-instrumentalise-their-members
passages.section: 3. Why such organisations instrumentalise their members
passages.text: “A thinker is invariably a sustainer of orderliness, whereas a ruler is invariably an exploiter of orderliness.” - MVD, Ch. 15

passages.heading: 3-why-such-organisations-instrumentalise-their-members
passages.section: 3. Why such organisations instrumentalise their members
passages.text: The sense of being instrumentalised is not a complaint about a particular boss or regime. It is the predictable signature of any organisation whose organising principle is fear or accumulation, because such a principle requires some members to be net-extracted-from so that others (or the system) can be net-secured. This is the failure of Objective 1.

passages.heading: 4-why-such-organisations-do-not-sustain
passages.section: 4. Why such organisations do not sustain
passages.text: 4. Why such organisations do not sustain

passages.heading: 4-why-such-organisations-do-not-sustain
passages.section: 4. Why such organisations do not sustain
passages.text: Fear-and-accumulation is not merely unkind; it is structurally fragile. This is the failure of Objective 2.

passages.heading: 4-why-such-organisations-do-not-sustain
passages.section: 4. Why such organisations do not sustain
passages.text: Fear-based collectivity is animal-order, and dissolves when the fear passes:

passages.heading: 4-why-such-organisations-do-not-sustain
passages.section: 4. Why such organisations do not sustain
passages.text: “The semblance of collectivity among animals is generally observed only in situations of fear. Under no circumstances is such collectivity observed in activities of study, production, or the maintenance of orderliness.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 4-why-such-organisations-do-not-sustain
passages.section: 4. Why such organisations do not sustain
passages.text: “A person may remain restrained by the fear of livelihood for some time, but eventually, they shed that fear. The end of slavery in history exemplifies this. … neither fear nor temptation can be the basis of orderliness, as they are unacceptable to humans.” - JV

passages.heading: 4-why-such-organisations-do-not-sustain
passages.section: 4. Why such organisations do not sustain
passages.text: Accumulation breeds suspicion, and suspicion breeds conflict: “War has always been driven by suspicion, mistrust, apprehension, coercion, bribery” (SB, Ch. 6); “Profit and loss constitute a relentless cycle that not only fails to secure humans but also destroys everything in its path” (JV).

passages.heading: 4-why-such-organisations-do-not-sustain
passages.section: 4. Why such organisations do not sustain
passages.text: The sustainability claim is stated decisively:

passages.heading: 4-why-such-organisations-do-not-sustain
passages.section: 4. Why such organisations do not sustain
passages.text: “Resolution is the very foundation of sustainability.” - SB, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 4-why-such-organisations-do-not-sustain
passages.section: 4. Why such organisations do not sustain
passages.text: “There is no sustainment of sociality without the tradition of coexistence.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 4-why-such-organisations-do-not-sustain
passages.section: 4. Why such organisations do not sustain
passages.text: An organisation does not last because it accumulates the most resources or commands the most force. It lasts because it produces resolution (members understand why and how they live and work together) and lives a tradition of coexistence (members complement rather than extract from each other). Resources and security are outputs of such an order, not its foundation.

passages.heading: 4-why-such-organisations-do-not-sustain
passages.section: 4. Why such organisations do not sustain
passages.text: This fragility is not only a moral observation but a structural one built into the template of coexistence. Every assembly — molecule, body, or organisation — persists in its natural state while its relationships are being fulfilled, and declines in its excited state when they are not (SB, p. 14; The Ontology of Coexistence §1.8). What is special about human organisations is that they sit at the knowledge order — the one tier where recognition and fulfilment are not automatic but must be achieved through understanding, evaluation, and choice, and therefore the one tier of nature that can actually fail (JV, p. 47; The Ontology of Coexistence §1.8). A molecule cannot mis-evaluate its bonds; an organisation can. Fear and accumulation are two ways of holding an assembly together without fulfilling the relationships inside it — that is, of pinning it in a permanently excited state. Such an organisation lasts only as long as the external pressure that holds it does.

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: 5. The alternative basis: coexistence

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: 5.1 Coexistence as the binding principle

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: “Resolution Centred Materialism is coexistence only.” - SB, Ch. 7

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: “For an organisation, commonness of cause and goal is necessary. For its sustainment, commonness of the program is also necessary.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: A durable organisation thus needs a shared cause (why we exist), shared goal (what we are for), and shared programme (how we live it daily) — the very condition the texts state for deliberate, knowledge-order assemblies (MVD, p. 55). The binding is not contract or command but duty and dedication: “The fulfilment of sociality is through duty and dedication … Otherwise, its decline occurs” (MVD, Ch. 4). The glue is trust:

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: “Trust is the act of fulfilling the inherent expectation of values in mutuality.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: And the positive formula:

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: “The foundational basis of sociality in awakened humans is living in resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: “Coexistence means living with complementarity. Fearlessness is trust in the present. Prosperity is producing in excess of our family’s needs. Resolution is living with justice.” - JV

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: These four — resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, coexistence — are not this paper’s shorthand but the darshan’s stated human goal, what awakened sociality evidences when the relational cycle closes, distinguished throughout from what coexistence merely provisions (The Ontology of Coexistence §1.13).

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: Note the precision of the term this paper turns on: the basis is not coexistence as sentiment, slogan, or mere peaceableness, but understood coexistence — coexistence that each member has studied and verified for themselves. §6 unpacks what this understanding consists of and how it is reached.

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: 5.2 Organisational design: ten-tier governance and two policies

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: The same principle scales from individual to family to society to nation to undivided world: “a family is an integral part of the undivided society, while an individual is an integral part of a family” (MVD, Ch. 14). It is implemented as family-based self-organising orderliness — ten-tier self-governance from family assembly up to world family assembly (MVD, Ch. 4).

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: How that scaling works is precise in the template. Units glue into a larger unit only when they are genuinely complementary and the result is a compound — a new unit with its own conduct — not a mere mixture in which each part keeps its own conduct unchanged (MVD, p. 42; SB, pp. 75–76). A set of individuals bound only by contract or fear is a mixture; a family or team that shares cause, goal, and programme is a compound. And the gluing succeeds only where the parts agree on what they share — the same members and the same values, without contradictory demands placed on them (How Undivided Society Is Established §5). Where two units place contradictory expectations on a shared person, the larger unit is forced to collapse. This is the structural reason the small unit must be oriented toward the larger whole rather than toward sectarian self-interest.

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: SB specifies the working machinery at the local tier: the village council nominates five self-governance working committees, each with defined roles:

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: “There will be five such committees: 1. Education-Sanskar Committee 2. Justice-Security Committee 3. Health-Restraint Committee 4. Production-Work Committee 5. Exchange-Reserve Committee. Each committee will have clearly defined roles and responsibilities.” - SB, Ch. 8

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: The five names are the four-fold goal made administrative: education-sanskar transmits understanding (§6); justice-security holds relationships and protection together; health-restraint covers the body and self-regulation; production-work delivers prosperity; exchange-reserve circulates goods without the profit-motive.

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: By design, two policies operate together, not in rivalry:

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: Dharma-niti (moral policy): orderliness for the right-use of body, mind, and wealth.

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: Rajya-niti (state policy): orderliness for the security of the same.

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: Each person desires both utilisation and protection; the darshan requires them to be integrated at every level from family to nation. They address different aspects of the same assets — not competing programmes.

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: Morality-versus-power — in its familiar form, religion-versus-state — is usually treated as an inherent rivalry. The darshan treats the rivalry as a symptom, not a definition: failure occurs when the two orders stop complementing each other and begin exploiting or interfering with each other and with the public:

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: “When these two orders start exploiting or interfering with each other … societal imbalance arises.” - MVD, Ch. 4

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: JV and SB name the present form of this split — moral authority lodged in religion, protection lodged in state, neither delivering orderliness. SB traces how religion-based politics and economics-based politics each anticipated complementarity between religion and state, or between economics and state, yet failed to secure orderliness in practice (SB, Ch. 2; synthesis).

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: JV adds that struggle-centred rule yields nothing apart from problems and suffering:

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: “Whatever revolts, rebellions, exploitations, and wars that humans have committed until now, these all were contrary to the principles of coexistence.” - JV, Ch. 1

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: Rule without understanding repeats the exploitation logic already seen in §3 — the ruler exploits orderliness; only the thinker sustains it.

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: 5.3 How coexistence answers both design objectives

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: Both design objectives of §1 are answered by the same move:

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: Objective 1 — members not instrumentalised: the organisation must add to the member, not subtract (Unit + Conducive unit); fulfil the values owed in each relationship; and hold to justice above mere legality. Justice here is not one value among values but the closure of the whole relational cycle — “recognising relationships, fulfilling values, evaluating, and achieving mutual satisfaction” (The Ontology of Coexistence §1.12.1; MVD, p. 311) — so that “Humane behaviour in mutuality itself is justice” (MVD, Ch. 1). Instrumentalisation is precisely this cycle left open: values unfulfilled or mis-evaluated, mutual satisfaction never reached. A member can therefore be treated entirely legally and still be exploited, because legality is not the closure of that cycle.

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: Objective 2 — sustainment: shared cause-goal-programme; resolution as foundation; prosperity through right-use rather than accumulation — “Material prosperity is accomplished only by adhering to the policy of ‘more production than the needs’” (MVD, Ch. 5), with “earning for expenditure” as non-accumulation (MVD, Ch. 10) and a cyclical economics (JV); and transmission across generations through education-sanskar — “This is how understanding flows in tradition. Ignorance cannot flow in tradition” (JV).

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: The two objectives are not in tension. Extraction-based systems must trade member welfare against growth; a coexistence-based system avoids the trade-off because the member’s flourishing is the organisation’s strength.

passages.heading: 5-the-alternative-basis-coexistence
passages.text: Dimension Fear / accumulation basis Coexistence basis Why people join Escape a threat; secure a scarce object Fulfil values in relationships; live with resolution Binding force Fear, temptation, command, contract Shared cause + goal + programme; trust; duty View of the member Means (net-extracted-from) End (net-nurtured) Economy Profit, accumulation, hoarding Right-use, production beyond need, cyclical Failure mode Dissolves when fear passes or accumulation stalls Fragile only if understanding is not transmitted Longevity basis Force and resources (external) Resolution and tradition of coexistence (internal)

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: Everything above rests on the load-bearing phrase introduced in §5.1: organisations founded on understood coexistence. This is not a figure of speech. In the darshan, “understanding coexistence” names a definite cognitive achievement with definite content, a definite method, and definite tests — and it is deliberately contrasted with belief, sentiment, agreement, and mystical experience.

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: 6.1 What is to be understood

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: Coexistence here is not tolerance, compromise, or “getting along.” It is a claim about the structure of reality: existence is units submerged in all-pervading space — distinct, energised, and related — and the four natural orders (material, bio, animal, and knowledge order) are mutually complementary (The Ontology of Coexistence §§1.1, 1.5). To understand coexistence is to know the darshan’s three inseparable areas of complete knowledge (The Ontology of Coexistence §1.13):

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: Existence — reality as coexistence; the complementarity of all orders

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: Jeevan — the conscious self, distinct from the body, that desires happiness and is satisfied only by understanding

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: Humane conduct — the values, character, and ethics that follow for a being who lives among other such beings

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: This is why “shared belief” cannot substitute for it. A belief locates the bond in an object of faith; understanding locates it in a recognisable structure of reality that each member can examine. The first divides humankind into sects; the second cannot, because what is understood is the same for everyone — “Humankind is united in the right and divided in the wrong” (MVD, Ch. 16).

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: 6.2 How it is reached: study, not belief or command

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: The darshan insists this understanding is teachable — open to examination, not reserved for the initiated or granted by grace:

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: “According to the idealistic scriptures and the mystery-based God-centric contemplation knowledge and tradition, the knowledge is unmanifest and ineffable. According to Madhyasth Darshan, the knowledge is manifest, effable, and understandable through studying, and its evidence becomes accessible to all through behaviour.” - MVD, The Alternative

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: “The alternative path is - perform study, attain mastery, then evidence it in living.” - JV, Ch. 1

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: The method is a sequence: study (adhyayan — sustained engagement with the proposal, guided by someone who already lives it), contemplation (turning the proposal over against one’s own observation and natural acceptance), understanding (the point where every why and how is answered — which is what the darshan means by resolution), and finally evidence in living (pramaan — the understanding showing up as justice, trust, and right-use in actual relationships). In the ontology’s terms this is the knowledge-order cycle knowing → believing → recognising → fulfilling: what a member unfolds (gyan udghatan) is not a private conviction but the relationships already built into coexistence, brought into lived conduct (The Ontology of Coexistence §§1.11, 1.13). The teaching is offered as a proposal to be verified, never as a command to be obeyed: each person checks it against what is naturally acceptable to them and validates it in their own living.

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: 6.3 How one knows it has been understood

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: Three tests separate understanding from its substitutes:

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: Resolution, not residue. Belief survives unanswered questions; understanding does not begin until they are answered. If “why coexistence?” still needs authority, fear, or incentive to back it, it has not been understood.

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: Communicability. What is understood can be made understandable to another. Mystery, by the darshan’s definition, cannot — which is why it transmits as allegiance instead of knowledge.

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: Evidence in behaviour. The decisive test is conduct: fulfilment of values in relationships, right-use of resources, production beyond need. An understanding that changes nothing in behaviour is, on this view, not yet understanding. This is the template’s self-evidencing closure: realisation counts as complete knowledge only when it is evidenced in conduct and made transmissible, never as private conviction alone (MVD, p. 12; The Ontology of Coexistence §1.11).

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: 6.4 Why every member must understand — and what this means for organisations

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: This is the organisational crux. In belief-based and command-based organisations, the “understanding” is held centrally — by the priesthood, the founder, the ideology, the management — and members participate by trust in authority. The darshan’s design forbids this delegation: resolution must live in each member, because trust is “fulfilling the inherent expectation of values in mutuality” (MVD, Ch. 4), and mutuality cannot be outsourced.

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: Hence two structural consequences already met above:

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: Education-sanskar is the central institution, not an auxiliary one: “Education-sanskar is the only source of enlightenment and definitive understanding” (SB, Ch. 4). An organisation of understood coexistence is, before anything else, a teaching-and-learning organisation — “This is how understanding flows in tradition. Ignorance cannot flow in tradition” (JV).

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: The family is the first site of verification. Relationships in the family are where values are first recognised, fulfilled, and evaluated — which is why the darshan’s self-organising orderliness is family-based rather than individual-based or state-based.

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: This also explains the failure modes catalogued earlier. Organisations decay precisely at the point where understanding stops being transmitted and is replaced by its cheaper substitutes — belief in the founder, fear of the rule, or incentive of the pay-off. The darshan’s claim is that no organisational structure can compensate for that substitution, and no structure is needed where it has not occurred.

passages.heading: 6-what-it-takes-to-understand-coexistence
passages.section: 6. What it takes to understand coexistence
passages.text: The template states this sharply. At the material, biological, and animal orders an assembly transmits its method of composition automatically — by constitution, seed, or lineage — but at the knowledge order the only available carrier is education-sanskar, and it carries understanding alone (JV, pp. 48–49). Because human assembly is the one tier where the relational cycle can fail, a human organisation is “built and sustained only by an unbroken transmission of understanding” (JV, p. 47). That is why a coexistence-based organisation is not merely an organisation that happens to run a school; it is one whose survival mechanism is the school.

passages.heading: 7-modern-organisational-forms-in-brief
passages.text: 7. Modern organisational forms in brief

passages.heading: 7-modern-organisational-forms-in-brief
passages.text: The darshan predates these modern forms and does not name them; this section applies its criteria to them. Modern forms line up on a spectrum by what binds members, from extraction toward coexistence:

passages.heading: 7-modern-organisational-forms-in-brief
passages.text: Modern form Organised around Darshan’s reading Shareholder firm; platform/gig Return on capital; transaction volume Purest accumulation order; relationship replaced by transaction Bureaucratic state; command economy Authority; central plan Power-centric rule; replacing private owners with state planners changes who extracts, not whether extraction is the principle Liberal democracy; stakeholder/ESG firm Consent, rights; multi-stakeholder value Better form, same basis — consent regulates exploitation but legality is not justice; “a nexus of votes and money” (MVD, Preface) Cooperatives; self-management (Teal) Shared ownership; distributed authority Strong echo of self-organising orderliness and “values and evaluation” over “fear and temptation” (JV); but bounded to one firm, market-embedded, no transmission mechanism Commons (Ostrom); peer production; mission orgs; intentional communities Shared resource, cause, or belief Closest in spirit — non-extraction, right-use, self-governance; but bounded to one domain or cause, funding/founder-fragile, or belief-based rather than understanding-based

passages.heading: 7-modern-organisational-forms-in-brief
passages.text: The best modern forms independently arrive at several darshan principles. What even they stop short of supplying together: a universal (non-sectarian) goal oriented to undivided society (How Undivided Society Is Established); resolution as understood coexistence rather than shared interest or belief; the four-fold goal (resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, coexistence) as a set; a transmission mechanism (education-sanskar) independent of founder or funding (Education and Sanskar); and an integrated cyclical economy of right-use rather than accumulation merely constrained by rules (Prosperity, Economics, and Right Use).

passages.heading: 8-practical-principles
passages.text: 8. Practical principles

passages.heading: 8-practical-principles
passages.text: An organisation that wants to sustain and not instrumentalise its people should:

passages.heading: 8-practical-principles
passages.text: Organise around an understood common cause and goal, not around a threat (§2, §5.1).

passages.heading: 8-practical-principles
passages.text: Make the programme common and explicit — sustainment requires shared how, not just shared why (§5.1).

passages.heading: 8-practical-principles
passages.text: Treat every internal relationship as value-bearing; disregarding the values owed (trust, fair return, respect, care) is exploitation by definition (§3).

passages.heading: 8-practical-principles
passages.text: Design for nurturing, not extraction (Unit + Conducive unit) (§3).

passages.heading: 8-practical-principles
passages.text: Replace fear and temptation with values and evaluation — compliance bought by fear or incentive is temporary (§4).

passages.heading: 8-practical-principles
passages.text: Hold to justice above mere legality (§5.3).

passages.heading: 8-practical-principles
passages.text: Aim for prosperity through right-use, not accumulation — produce beyond need, spend righteously, avoid profit-as-imbalance (§5.3).

passages.heading: 8-practical-principles
passages.text: Keep moral order and governance complementary, neither dominating the people (§5.2).

passages.heading: 8-practical-principles
passages.text: Transmit understanding through education-sanskar across generations (§6.4).

passages.heading: 8-practical-principles
passages.text: Orient the small unit toward the larger whole — family/team toward society and undivided society, not sectarian self-interest (§5.2).

passages.heading: 9-from-here-to-there-the-transition-path
passages.section: 9. From here to there: the transition path
passages.text: 9. From here to there: the transition path

passages.heading: 9-from-here-to-there-the-transition-path
passages.section: 9. From here to there: the transition path
passages.text: The darshan describes an end-state, not a reform programme for existing institutions. The texts do not prescribe how a fear- or accumulation-based organisation converts itself. But the darshan’s own logic implies a definite ordering, and it is worth making explicit. (This section is inference from the texts’ method, not quotation.)

passages.heading: 9-from-here-to-there-the-transition-path
passages.section: 9. From here to there: the transition path
passages.text: Understanding precedes structure. Since no organisational structure can compensate for the absence of understanding (§6.4), transition cannot begin with restructuring — new charters, new incentives, new org-charts on the old basis reproduce the old basis. It begins with members studying and verifying the proposal.

passages.heading: 9-from-here-to-there-the-transition-path
passages.section: 9. From here to there: the transition path
passages.text: Start at the scale where verification is possible. The family — or the smallest working team — is the first site where values can actually be recognised, fulfilled, and evaluated (§6.4). Larger tiers federate what already works; they cannot conjure it.

passages.heading: 9-from-here-to-there-the-transition-path
passages.section: 9. From here to there: the transition path
passages.text: Education-sanskar before governance reform. The first committee is the teaching one (§5.2). A transmission mechanism that does not depend on the founder must exist before the founder’s understanding can outlive them.

passages.heading: 9-from-here-to-there-the-transition-path
passages.section: 9. From here to there: the transition path
passages.text: Evidence attracts; command does not. The method is study → mastery → evidence in living (JV, §6.2). An organisation demonstrating resolution, prosperity, and fearlessness recruits by being visibly worth joining — the darshan’s answer to “how does this spread?” is demonstration, not conquest or decree.

passages.heading: 9-from-here-to-there-the-transition-path
passages.section: 9. From here to there: the transition path
passages.text: The implied sequence — understand, live it small, teach it, federate — also explains why the darshan is unimpressed by reforms that begin at the top: they change who holds the structure, not what the structure is organised around.

passages.heading: 10-limits-and-open-questions
passages.text: 10. Limits and open questions

passages.heading: 10-limits-and-open-questions
passages.text: The diagnosis explains a real, recurring pattern — fear- or accumulation-founded organisations do treat members as instruments and do fracture when the founding fear recedes or accumulation stalls. The definition of exploitation as disregarding values in a relationship gives a usable test for whether people are being instrumentalised, and the resolution-plus-coexistence thesis dissolves the apparent trade-off between member welfare and durability.

passages.heading: 10-limits-and-open-questions
passages.text: There are however following questionable points in the claims made by the Madhyasth Darshan:

passages.heading: 10-limits-and-open-questions
passages.text: Fear has legitimate uses. Grouping against genuine threats is sometimes necessary. The defensible version of the claim is that threat-avoidance cannot be the foundational organising principle, not that safety-driven cooperation is wrong.

passages.heading: 10-limits-and-open-questions
passages.text: Accumulation versus prudent reserve. “Earning for expenditure” and “production more than needs” partly anticipate the need for reserves, but the boundary between healthy surplus and harmful hoarding is left to judgement.

passages.heading: 10-limits-and-open-questions
passages.text: No theory of bad-faith actors. The design assumes members who understand or are willing to study. The texts name a Justice-Security committee (SB, Ch. 8) but give no procedure for the member who persistently exploits, dissents, or refuses to participate — no account of adjudication, sanction, exit, or expulsion. Institutional justice and statutory order are deferred to the planned Governance, Justice, and Undivided Society study, but for an organisational design this remains the largest practical gap: every real organisation eventually meets the person its theory says should not exist.

passages.heading: 10-limits-and-open-questions
passages.text: Dependence on the ontology. The deepest premises — jeevan, awakening, existence-as-coexistence — are asserted, not empirically demonstrated. A secular designer can adopt nearly the whole practical programme on organisational grounds alone while remaining agnostic about the metaphysics; a strength for adoption, a weakness for anyone seeking a proven first principle.

passages.heading: 11-comparison-with-advaita-vedanta
passages.text: 11. Comparison with Advaita Vedanta

passages.heading: 11-comparison-with-advaita-vedanta
passages.text: A natural question for an Indian reader: does Advaita Vedanta, the oldest non-dual tradition, already offer a basis for building a prosperous society? The two are close relatives — Shri A. Nagraj came through the Vedic/Vedantic stream, and Madhyasth Darshan defines itself partly against Advaita’s formula “Brahma satya, jagat mithya” (MVD, The Alternative). The full metaphysical comparison — Brahman and mithya, the two truths, and where the traditions’ categories do and do not map — is developed in The Ontology of Coexistence §2 and §5.7; here the question is narrowly organisational, measured against this paper’s two design objectives. (Beyond the three primary sources this draws on Shankara (AV), Vivekananda’s “Practical Vedanta” (SV), and Rambachan (ATR); readings are marked interpretation where they exceed the texts.)

passages.heading: 11-comparison-with-advaita-vedanta
passages.text: Advaita is not socially empty. If tat tvam asi — the self of every being is Brahman — then there is ontologically no “Other” to exploit, arguably a stronger anti-exploitation premise than any rights theory; nishkama karma and lokasamgraha give a reason to serve rather than accumulate; and modern readings (Vivekananda’s “potential divinity” of every being, Rambachan’s “not-two is not one”) built activism against caste and ecological harm, sustained by real institutions such as the Ramakrishna Mission. On the darshan’s own spectrum (§7), Advaita-inspired organisations belong with the closest, non-extractive forms.

passages.heading: 11-comparison-with-advaita-vedanta
passages.text: Measured against the two objectives, though, classical Advaita falls short in identifiable ways. Its goal is individual moksha, not organisational: community, family, and production belong to the world the renunciant turns from, so an organisation is at best instrumental to liberation, never the locus of value. “Jagat mithya” undercuts prosperity — a philosophy cannot found a prosperous society on a premise that devalues the domain in which prosperity occurs; even sympathetic reformers concede pre-reform Vedanta became “a philosophy of escape” (SV). The two-truths doctrine let perfect equality at the absolute level coexist with caste hierarchy at the empirical level for over a millennium — interpretation: a unity that does not bind conduct fails the darshan’s test that understanding become evidence in behaviour. Transmission ran through guru-shishya lineage and monastic qualification (adhikara) for a renunciant minority — the opposite of an education-sanskar meant to reach all through ordinary families. And Advaita specifies no economy, governance, or family order — no counterpart to “commonness of cause and goal … and of the program” (MVD, Ch. 4).

passages.heading: 11-comparison-with-advaita-vedanta
passages.text: The decisive divergence is metaphysical and has direct organisational consequences. Advaita resolves plurality upward into one reality without a second: relationships, like the related persons, are ultimately appearance. Madhyasth Darshan refuses this move — existence is units submerged in all-pervading space, distinct and related. Plurality is real, therefore relationships are real, therefore the values inherent in them (trust, respect, justice) are real and their fulfilment or violation is real. That is what makes “exploitation = disregarding values in a relationship” a usable organisational test rather than a provisional truth awaiting dissolution.

passages.heading: 11-comparison-with-advaita-vedanta
passages.text: Dimension Advaita Vedanta Madhyasth Darshan Ultimate reality Brahman, one without a second; world is mithya Existence as coexistence; world is real and perpetual Human goal Individual moksha through self-knowledge Resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, coexistence — lived in relationship Basis against exploitation No “Other” exists (ontological unity) Values in real relationships; nurturing vs extraction Status of relationships Empirically valid, ultimately appearance Constitutive of reality; locus of justice Prosperity Not a goal; renunciation idealised Defined goal: production beyond need, right-use Organisational design None (monastic orders as exception) Ten-tier family-based self-organising orderliness Transmission Guru-shishya, monastic, qualified few Education-sanskar for all, through families

passages.heading: 11-comparison-with-advaita-vedanta
passages.text: Advaita supplies the strongest possible premise for human unity — there is finally no Other — but not the programme for human organisation; its strongest social readings (SV, ATR) are modern efforts to extract from non-duality what Madhyasth Darshan builds in from the start: a real world, real relationships, a defined economy, and a transmission mechanism for all. The darshan keeps Advaita’s insistence on human dignity and the unity of existence while replacing “one without a second” with “coexistence,” so that unity can bind conduct and production rather than dissolve them. This comparison is between Advaita’s historical record and the darshan’s design principles: the latter has not been tested at civilisational scale, so the claim is about coherence and completeness of design, not a proven track record.

passages.heading: 12-conclusion
passages.text: 12. Conclusion

passages.heading: 12-conclusion
passages.text: Humans do not have to organise around fear, food, protection, belief, or accumulation. Those are the bases history happened to use, and they are precisely why organisations exploit their members and eventually decay. The durable, non-exploitative basis is organisation around understood coexistence — shared cause, goal, and programme; fulfilment of values in relationships; right-use rather than accumulation; and a tradition that transmits this understanding across generations.

passages.heading: 12-conclusion
passages.text: Fear + accumulation → members instrumentalised → organisation decays Coexistence + resolution → members fulfilled → organisation sustains

passages.heading: 12-conclusion
passages.text: The contribution of this view is to collapse two problems usually treated separately — keeping people happy and keeping the institution alive — into a single design choice about what an organisation is organised around. Choose fear or accumulation, and the two goals fight each other. Choose understood coexistence, and the same principle that fulfils the member also sustains the whole.
